pitch_detail.notes: Starts up the gully left of a fallen tree. Easy scrambly ground with a long runout of about 15 m before the first bolt, then angle left and up, cross a gravel ramp rightward and come back left onto the ledge. Gear protects after the first bolt. The belay is on that ledge right of the chimney; do not climb past it by mistake. Rock is loose.

Steep and enjoyable. Cross the chimney leftward onto the arete beside it; a hard-to-spot piton sits roughly three metres above the belay and to the left. A crack taking a #4 cam leads to a bolt a few metres higher, after which bolts and pitons guard the whole arete. Belay on a roomy ledge, or continue to a two-bolt anchor above the gravel ledge, taking care not to rain gravel on your second.

Easy but loose ground up to a two-bolt belay just right of and above a tree. Gear is poor and there are some runouts, much like the first pitch. The original line short-roped rightward to easier ground, which this longer pitch replaces.

A short pitch added to the route. Go straight up, then left around a feature using underclings, to a two-bolt anchor just below the big island of trees. Gear is good here, but the top-out onto gravel feels insecure.

Walk over to the face and begin beside an evident weakness, just to its left. Clean rock with good gear placements throughout; the bolted anchor lies a little left. The treed ledge below is steep and gravelly, so scramble it carefully.
Keep following the crack system, where an old wooden block is jammed. After roughly 20 m, step left around a roof, then go directly up to a bolted anchor on a small ledge. Good beginner trad.

The line is less clear. Go up and a little right, passing a corner on your left and some old pitons on a water-worn wall. Head for a small tree, pass it over gravelly ledge, and the bolted anchor is to your left. Easy ground under the tree is runout with poor gear. Slinging the tree as a directional protects your second from pebbles.

Begin straight up with a runout but easy start; a #2 cam fits in the worn groove. Head for the block holding a vertical crack. Two bolts, set close together, guard the short crux between them: mostly friction on small chips. Best rock of the route; the anchor is bolted, on the ledge.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with grades, lengths and notes. The stored count of 8 matches; the route is also done as 6 or 7 pitches by short-roping. Left out the alternate walk-off and summit-ridge info.
review.other_findings: Description allows 6, 7 or 8 pitches depending on short-roping; stored count is 8. Bolted anchors throughout.

pitch_detail.notes: Fairly easy but insecure mixed ground above the snow gully. Belay on a fixed pin anchor beneath the start of the ice chimney.

Follow the chimney, using ice in the back and rock on the sides. Pass under a large chockstone to a fixed anchor near the 60 m mark. A second big chockstone sits above; better to climb a couple more metres and build a belay on a ledge higher and left, which keeps the belayer safer for the next lead.

Climb beneath the chockstone. Above, a choice opens up between a possibly iced slab to the left or two steeper cracks on the right. The reporting party took loose ground right toward the cracks and stopped at a fixed pin and nut belay.

Not climbed by the reporting party. Go up either the slab on the left or the steep cracks on the right, which join again above. Grade is uncertain, somewhere between M4 and M6, and the length is thought to be under 60 m.
Not climbed by the reporting party. Past a final bulge to the ridge; thought to be under 60 m and roughly M5. Parties are believed to rappel from fixed gear from about here.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. P1-P3 were climbed and described firmly; P4 and P5 were not climbed by the reporter, so their grades and lengths are left out and the notes hedge. Left out the approach, the snow gully below P1 and the descent talk.
review.other_findings: Descent is reported as rappels from fixed gear, not confirmed.

pitch_detail.notes: Face climbing left of the large corner on reasonable rock with good jugs, angling left. The anchor is up and left on vertical ground, so linking brings heavy drag. A 5.10b alternative with 10 bolts begins a few metres left: a slab, a shallow roof, then solid limestone to the same anchor.
Loose rock up to an anchor roughly 10 m under the third pitch belay.
A scramble on easy ground to the next belay station.
Trend right on steeper rock with one harder move on a side pull. The anchor is low, beneath an overhang.

Up and right to a bolt, then back left to pull over a small roof past two bolts on good holds, which is the 5.9 section. Continue up and right through broken steps past three more bolts. To skip the roof, sling the first bolt long and move right past another bolt and up easy steps: 5.7, four bolts.
Steep steps, linking one bolt to the next.
Up and right through steep ground with a couple of awkward moves, including an airy step right that is close-bolted. Long alpine slings help.
A very short pitch to a ledge strewn with loose rock, anchor at the base of the yellow wall. Rather than linking, bring your partner up; that limits drag and rockfall.
Begins right of the anchor: ascend the steep gully, working out right, then return left across a slab to a big ledge with an anchor. Likely the best pitch on the climb.
Short steep moves lead to a big ledge with the final anchor. Two bolts higher up lead nowhere unless you build a tree anchor.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches with grade, length, bolt count and notes. Added the 5.10b alternate start to P1 notes and the 5.7 roof bypass to P5. Left out the ridge continuation above the route and its descent. No rappel station table: the text says the route is rap-equipped but does not list stations.
review.other_findings: Some accounts reportedly mention an 11th pitch; text describes 10 and the stored count is 10.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the buttress crest, easing slightly right at a break, past bolts to gentler ground and a two-bolt belay on a rock outcrop. The start has no anchor; spot the first bolt about 5 m up and left.

Scramble over a small roll and climb slabby ground with three bolts, then a blocky face beside a poor-looking corner (two bolts). Angle up and left over ramps and scree ledges, pass an intermediate anchor, and finish at a higher two-bolt belay.
Traverse up and left toward a loose, wet-looking corner but avoid it, instead climbing the slabby face about 10 m to the right on a line of four bolts to a big ledge.
Go up and right along the ledge, round the corner, then scramble up and right across scree to a one-bolt belay on a blob of rock.

Begin in the wide groove over the belay, first on its right side, then directly up; careful, and doubles are useful. Traverse left along the ledge above, clip two bolts, and drift left into a steep recess. Follow the groove above, trending up and right, to a ledge with a two-bolt anchor.
Walk across scree and rubble to a single-bolt anchor placed where the ridge line hits the cliff.

Start left of the belay, passing a slight bulge to reach a good hold beside a bolt. The scoop above leads to another short steep wall and bulge, the crux, with an anchor soon after. Continue beyond it up the right-hand corner, three more bolts, then traverse left on a ledge that widens to a comfy two-bolt belay.
From the belay go left and make a slabby move to the second bolt. Then up, around the corner to the left, and straight on to scree, finishing at a two-bolt anchor on the rock overhead.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with lengths, grades and bolt counts. Left out the approach and the ridge walk to the summit.
review.other_findings: Rappelling the route is possible with double ropes but anchors lack rings.

pitch_detail.notes: Straight up to a high first bolt, then a short right-trending hand crack. After it step left to another bolt, avoiding loose fourth-class ground on the right. Belay on the prominent ledge. One piece of 1-2 inch gear supplements the two bolts.

Fine face climbing up and left on a bolt line. In the little alcove past the last bolt, put in the only gear the pitch needs (a finger-size piece and a 3 inch piece), then ease up and slightly left past the hard part to the belay. Long slings reduce drag at the mid-pitch traverse.
Easy climbing with little gear. The belay is exposed to rockfall from low-angle terrain above. Go up and slightly right, then sharply left when level with the next belay, which is directly above.

A high first bolt, reached from the ledge system on the left. Straight up the right-facing corner past two more bolts; after the crux a key 0.75 cam (with a finger cam as backup) leads to another bolt. After the fourth bolt step right to wider cracks and follow them up left to the belay ledge.

Technical and sustained. Go left on a 3-4 inch cam for about 5 m, then back right to a bolt. Straight up to the steep wall base, left up finger cracks, then right onto the main face a few metres before a big loose-looking corner and up the headwall on bolts. Two flakes midway are the crux; they have been hammered on, so tread lightly. A medium nut helps before the anchor, and long draws help early on.
Step right to a hidden bolt, then up and right to the ridgeline. On the ridge, follow wider cracks up and left to the belay. Gear up to 4 inches.
Scale the top of the pinnacle above (easy), descend a few metres on its left, then traverse left past a bolt to the broad ledge under the Diamond. Gear to 1 inch.

Aim for the main off-width and the bolt below it. Three bolts up, wander through broken cracks a few metres off to the off-width's right until a small stance, which the alternative joins. Face cracks and a small roof come next, then the off-width itself up to the next ledge. The alternative, also 5.10- and 40 m, climbs a hand crack from the lower belay, clips a pin then a bolt, and a seam takes you back into the main line. Gear to 4 inches.
Climb the prominent cracks out left, then after a ledge go steeply up a thin dihedral, which is the cruxy part; small nuts help there. Gear to 4 inches.

Keep climbing cracks on the ridge's left side. High on the pitch a steep off-width corner takes hidden cams and two bolts. At the exposed stance above, step right to the ridge and a bolt, then go on to the top of the Diamond. You can skip the off-width by taking looser rock on the ridge.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches with grades, lengths, bolt counts and protection. Pitch 8 has two options, both 5.10- and 40 m; the entry covers the main one and mentions the alternative. No rappel table: the text only describes rappel reversal loosely, not station by station.
review.other_findings: Row grade 5.12- matches the hardest pitch (P5).

pitch_detail.notes: Shares its first anchors with the neighbouring route Walk of Ages. An independent first pitch may exist about 10 m to the left.
The crux. Go straight at the second bolt rather than left onto the neighbouring line. Thoughtful, involving climbing on mostly small holds, with big jugs as a reward.
Interesting movement. A couple of delicate balancey moves at the start lead to a welcome big jug after some slightly precarious steps.
Fairly straightforward, with few real footholds. Good views from the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with grades only; the text gives no lengths or bolt counts. P1 grade is second-hand and the independent-start note is hedged.
review.other_findings: Reporters thought it harder than the 5.10 they first expected; stored grade 5.11b matches pitch 2.

pitch_detail.notes: A sport pitch on a single 70 m rope with 13 draws; the hardest part is near the top. It can be split by veering left at the halfway point to a rappel station, sensible if the upper section worries you. An extendable draw or two is handy.

Short, scrambly and soloable at around 5.3, to a pair of bolts on the next headwall. Those bolts serve for rappelling or for belaying a second. From there trend right under the headwall to a flat spot among bushes.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches: the long sport pitch and the short scramble pitch. The stored count is 3, but the text describes only the first two as pitches and the rest as a long scramble; no third pitch invented. No rappel table: only 2 stations 35 m apart are mentioned for the upper cliff.
review.other_findings: Stored 3 pitches; text describes 1 sport pitch, a short easy pitch, then fifth-class scrambling to the summit.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the southwest side of the arete and use broken features to aim at the large right-facing corner with a continuous crack. Ledges appear at about 35 and 40 m; the first is marked by a big flake on the right. Stem the flake to a slightly higher ledge with more gear. A tempting horizontal horn there is loose, so do not use it for the belay.

Either stay with the corner system or take a thin seam to a small roof. A tips-size seam to the roof, then much easier ground rightward for half a rope, ends on a ledge that is still west of the arete.

Shift the belay across the arete: gain about 2 m, then traverse roughly 5 m east to the foot of parallel cracks. Excellent but fiddly cracks; keep a red offset nut for the spot beneath the roof. Get past the roof, then easier ground with long gaps in gear.
Progressively easier ground; technical climbing is over and the rack can go. Scramble the final 50 m to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. The text gives 35-40 m per pitch, so lengths are left out. Left out the descent and approach.
review.other_findings: Row grade 5.9 but pitch 3 is 5.10b; the writer suggests the original line may take an easier left-facing corner farther right.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on thin ice into a steep rock slot, then a snow ledge up to a fixed pin anchor on the right. Rock gear can help near the top if the ice is thin.
Left, then thin ice that gets better with height; a sheltered alcove belay.
A steep ice shield rises from the belay, then angle up and left to a comfortable alcove belay.
Steep, unbroken ice, finishing at v-threads under the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with lengths converted from feet (190, 130, 110, 170 ft). No pitch grades are given, so none written.

pitch_detail.notes: Start about 10 m left of the ridge; a bolt shows up around 10 m high and another shortly after. Grooves and cracks lead to a large ledge where a bolted station sits against the back wall. Keep the rope off the scree there.
Straight up from the anchor along the weakness to a right-facing corner, then grooves up and left to the belay.
Easy ground up and right to a short left-facing corner, back left toward obvious cracks above the belay, then an easier corner system trending up and left.

A thin crack up the left-facing corner over the belay, then another corner and a face crack on the right-hand wall, to easier ground and on toward a right-facing corner with a good crack. As it begins to overhang, bolt protection leads rightward toward the arete; once past it, the next anchor is visible up-left on a good stance.

Straight up past bolts to a bouldery crux. As bolts end, two 5.11- ways reach the anchor: up left into a corner with a bolt for the exit, or right around a pillar and up thin cracks below a roof. Gear to 0.75.
Sustained, varied climbing from anchor to anchor along the bolts. One cam (0.4 or 0.5) fits in a good finger crack between the last three bolts, covering a long gap.
A short, obvious bolt line to the next ledge.
A rising bolted traverse left of the anchor leads to a striking finger crack that starts thin and widens to a big ledge at its top, with good gear. Gear to a #1 cam.
The crack above the anchor, trending right about halfway to a right-facing corner, to the top of the pillar.
Hand crack left of the belay, then a foot traverse back right past a bolt, and straight up the crack through the overhanging wall to a belay on top of the wall.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches with grade, length and bolt counts. All belays are bolted with rappel rings; no per-station rappel table written. Left out first-ascent story.
review.other_findings: P8 grade given as 5.12+/5.13-, consistent with stored 5.13a.

pitch_detail.notes: Up the corner with an awkward start, then traverse right at the top to another corner for the belay.
Keep following the corner through easy ledges to steeper moves. Belay on a small ledge on the arete, a good stance out of rockfall.

Of the two cracks above take the left one: good jams and stems up to a piton and a rusty bolt on the face. Difficult thin face moves then ease; step left into a groove, climb another easy crack and some ledges, and pull a bulge to a belay on a mossy ledge under a crack.
Do not go up. Step left around the corner, blind, and across a ledge to a groove or crack.

Easy up the groove to a steep crack with big stems and good jams on the left wall, to a ledge with a piton. Then up and left onto another ledge around the arete. The original line may have belayed at the piton and taken the easy crack above.

The Grimwall Traverse. Go up a steep crack to a ledge that leads leftward and follow it without protection. At its end a blank wall blocks the way, so commit to a shallow foot rail across to the far face and climb the steep, solid wall to a ledge under a roof. Reporters were off route on this stretch, so details are uncertain.

The Woodhead Chimney: right on poor rock to a chimney, hard entry, then to a roof with big blocks and good gear. Pull the roof on the left, stem to a ledge, and climb the loose steep wall above to a belay ledge on top.
Short corners to good rock heading left, then down-climb under a big corner to a good belay ledge.

Wide crack leading out left; awkward moves past a flake, with old fixed gear in the crack. At its top, move left over steep bulges to a slab and a crack, and belay beneath a roof on a semi-hanging stance.
Move up and right into an improbable-looking groove of good rock, avoid the roof on its right, and ramble to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches with grades and lengths. The writer admits being off route on two middle pitches, so P6-P7 notes are hedged. No bolt counts or anchors stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb in from the left or find holds directly to the first bolt. A varied, steep section, then pull around the arete and find the semi-hanging station out left.
An exposed traverse. Rock over just above the first bolt and keep below the rest of the bolt line, reaching the big ledge.

From the belay, climb up and right to a low crux built around a jug side-pull, then a sea of more side-pulls. Once atop the pillar, step hard right and exposed to more side-pulls rather than going straight for the anchor.
Move above the anchor then left to the first bolt. Thin friction slab, a traverse into a technical layback crack that grows into a large corner. Near its top, the station is on a ledge to the right.

Walk up from the belay to begin, avoiding hollow flakes on the left in the lower part. A ramp gains ledgy terrain where extending a bolt or two helps. Reach the big belay ledge via the tree; the dugout is only for the rope. This pitch cannot be rappelled.

Long. From the belay bolt beneath the corner, step off the pillar leftward to jugs, then side-pulls leftward to a committing rockover. Meander up and right, climb the big flake, then a thin horizontal traverse from the small white ledge, and one more crux sequence through the small roof.

Technical ramp start with a couple of concealed key holds. A press gets you to the horizontal crack; exiting it is the crux, so stand tall on tiny feet and find the best crimps. Then balancey, textured rock with huge exposure to the top of the wall; the anchor lies over the lip, past the final bolt.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches with grade, length and bolts. No rappel station table: the descent text is a route-description of two rappel lines, not a clean top-to-bottom station list, and P5 cannot be rappelled.

pitch_detail.notes: A low-angle slab, then big side-pulls to a layback crack. Ledges lead to a brief vertical crux with tiny feet. After the final clip, move left to the dugout, reach the belay ledge, then return right to the station.

Start by clipping the first bolt from the belay, then descend to the tree to begin; the belayer should unclip that bolt to cut drag. A technical traverse leads to a fun finish through the double-roof arete. Climb the solid rock left of the tree rather than wrestling it, then step across into the tree-house belay.

Wandering, exposed, with several cruxes. Some loose rock in the corner, capped by steep ground; step left for big side-pulls and underclings. After a rest, a bouldery move through a blue bulge leads to another tricky sequence.

A mega pitch ending on an exposed arete. Extending the bottom two bolts is wise. Past the ramp, cross the roof to the arete and follow it to a stance, then take the steep arete head on: a secure but hard-to-find stance lets you reach the higher clip, and the next bolt is just over the lip. Pulling on bolts all through the crux is not possible.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with grade, length and bolts. No rappel table: only a 70 m single rappel of the last pitch is described.

pitch_detail.notes: From the anchor in a corner left of the main ramp, climb to a steep exposed face. That is the crux, well protected by a shiny bolt. Above it continue along the ramp to the next anchor.
A shorter pitch with a slight left traverse, then up left of the chimney.

Up and right along the chimney to a sloping ledge beneath a steep, wide crack. It can be climbed at roughly 5.10- with a #2 and/or #3, short and well protected; otherwise take the corner to the right and then go back left to the next anchor.

Uncertain details. A low-angle left-facing corner protects well but needs a hard traverse right at the end, with heavy drag. The proper line probably trends right up steeper blocky terrain directly to the anchors.
Details are vague: go straight up, cross a gully to a face, then follow a crack that trends right toward where the main chimney feature ends, to an anchor at its edge.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. Writer recalls P4 and P5 only vaguely, so those notes are hedged and carry no grade. P3 has an optional 5.10- crack. Left out the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Shared with a harder neighbouring route. Steep vertical face onto a slab, with a runout of about 4 m after the fifth bolt; move left onto easy chossy rock to dodge a small roof. Alpine draws help on bolts 5 and 6. Technical, sustained climbing to the anchors. Rock is poorer here.
Go immediately left, not up and right, traversing seven bolts before climbing past the roof and up to the anchor. Staying low feels easier. Can be linked with the next pitch using alpine draws.
Cruisy slab climbing straight up to the next anchors under the steep wall. The belay is uncomfortable.

Long and steep with juggy, sustained sections, well bolted so expect to use most draws. Some optional crack moves higher, three bolts past the roof. Belay on the ledge above; the station has only a small foot rail.
Good holds and mellow climbing to a treed bench at the top.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. No rappel table: only the combined descent plan is given, not station by station.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy ice to the base of a steep pillar.
Steep ice for about 30 m, then a brief overhang (which may be pure ice in a good year) and an aesthetic ice goulotte, stretching the rope to a sheltered belay.
Snow and ice up to the base of the next long ice flow, with a deep chimney on the right.
A sustained slanting groove on the right edge of the ice gets you onto the flow. Belay there or carry on to where the ice ends.
The scrappy pitch. Where the ice ends, take the chimney on the right to a notch in the ridge, then back left to a second ridge with a good ledge belay. The upper corner can be seen from there.
Traverse right from the belay, then climb the striking quartzite corner. Belay on an obvious ledge on the right; keep a 0.4 cam for the anchor.
More corner climbing with good gear through a small overlap. Exit the corner, move up and right to a small ledge with a view of the northeast face.
Move right and follow the blunt ridge upward.
Follow a snow and ice gully on the right to the east ridge.

review.changed: Wrote 11 pitches; P3-P5 are given as one 180 m stretch of snow and ice so written as one entry labelled 3-5.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep, vibrating column leads to a vertical wall of ice that lessens in angle after about 10 m; then mostly WI4 to a right-hand belay.
Long stretch of good ice, ending at another belay on the right.
Steep slot filled with ice, leaning right, to the finish.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with grade and length.

pitch_detail.notes: The Postscriptum pillar to a hanging bolt belay, the only bolts on the climb.

Go to the top of the pillar for the Whipper Traverse, with interesting pitons (grade uncertain, possibly M6 or M7), or place a high screw and traverse right with a couple of M4/5 moves, skipping it. Then funky vertical ice until the angle eases to about 85 degrees.
Exposed WI5 climbing to a belay; there is sometimes a cave that makes a great belay spot.
Vertical ice to the top. Descent is by v-threads.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches, hedged because the writer climbed in easier conditions than the route's top grade. Only P1 length and P1/P3 grades are stated.
review.other_findings: Row grade WI7+ R applies in thin first-ascent conditions; the reporter found WI5+/6 in thicker ice.

pitch_detail.notes: A series of vertical steps leads to a curtain or pillars spilling over a small roof. Pass the roof and continue on steep ice to a belay left, beneath another overhang. The roof may be the crux.
Move right from the belay and climb vertical to slightly overhanging ice, then take the headwall, steep, to a right-hand belay below a small overhang. The overhang at the start may be the crux.
Step left from the belay to a steep column that may overhang slightly at the top.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with lengths. No pitch grades given, so none written; the crux location is described as uncertain.
review.other_findings: Approach ice is WI3 to a one-bolt belay.

skip_reasons.ab_morro_peak_spring_break: No per-pitch text: only a general description of a ledge system and a crux guess for pitch 2.
